name: WebAuthn Signal API
plain: Lets a site tell the passkey manager a credential is gone or its name changed.
meaning: Keeps the passkey list clean. Shows no data back to the site.

access.iframe: Same as top level; cross-origin iframes need a permissions policy where listed

data.metric: Lets a site tell the passkey manager a credential is gone or its name changed.

limits.headline: Can tell your passkey manager that a passkey is gone or renamed
limits.user_action: Nothing extra. It happens after you delete an account or change your username
can: Send a note that a passkey no longer works so the manager can hide it
Send a new username or display name so your passkey list stays tidy
cannot: See what passkeys your manager holds; it sends nothing back
Delete a passkey on its own; the manager decides
Work in Firefox, or in Safari before version 26
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge support it from version 132 and Safari from version 26; Firefox does not yet.

story.what_it_is: Lets a site tell your passkey manager that a passkey was removed or renamed.

marketing.name: Passkeys Signal API
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes it as a way to keep passkey lists up to date when an account or name changes.

story.for_you: You never see a prompt. When you delete a passkey on a site, your phone or password manager quietly removes it from its list too. The list stays tidy.
story.for_makers: Makers keep users from seeing stale or broken passkeys that cause failed sign ins. Fewer failures mean fewer help requests and cleaner security records.

use_cases.example: A game account page removes a deleted passkey from the player's list, so they are not offered a broken one at login.
A bank cleans up passkeys after a customer closes an account or changes their username.
A shop updates the name of a passkey when a person changes their email, so the list still makes sense.
A work app tells the manager to remove passkeys for a former employee's departed device.
A security team uses it to remove old keys after a suspected break in.
